en: Calling fortune down upon his head,
And easing their burdened hearts.
“The lord of Beijing has come,” they said,
And had it written in the chronicles.
High and low, old and young,
Women in white kerchiefs mingled with men.
In radiant Beijing
Countless festivities abounded.
By the Black Khan’s throne,
In the garden where he took his pleasure,
There was a narrow place no man could tread.
Beneath a dragon
Was a well called Zuu,
With twin clefts like a split palate,
Filled with countless portents.
The Zuu Well to which they took him
Had a dragon at its bottom,
Venomous toward every mighty foe.
It was a well of divination,
And terrible was its wrath.
At the bottom of that well
Was a sixty-headed dragon,
Whose breath drew things in from six fathoms away;
Exactly sixty heads it had,
The dragon in the Zuu Well.
Infants
And men by the tens of thousands
Were tested by the sorcerers
And taken to that Zuu Well.
Behold a wonder such as this:
The black dragon sporting in those waters—
Those destined to become loyal subjects
It left safe and sound,
But those destined to oppose the khagan
It sprayed with venom and sucked dry.
When they lowered him into the well,
The Zungtung attendants brought necklaces,
Plumes, and precious coral stones.
From the dragon’s very stench,
Many people fainted.
Yet great Teñir neither died nor vanished,
But emerged unharmed.
Fearing someone might harm him,
They enclosed him behind ninety layers of iron chambers,
Not letting even a breath of wind touch him.
No one with corrupt speech,
No one with an evil eye,
Not a single soul was allowed near;
Thus they reared him thereafter.
They wrapped and covered
His radiant good fortune with ritual care,
And had him raised without seeing sunlight.
“If he survives, he will become great,” they said;
“When angered, he will drive the world
Before him and suck it dry.
For the khagan whom none can withstand,
The towering Mount Kap has arisen.
For Beijing, beyond the reach of the Flood,
Your daring Chyng has become mighty.”
Thus Chyngteñir
Was entered into the chronicles,
And among the many people of China’s forty tribes
He became known as Chyngteñir.
No living soul could withstand his fury,
No people could match his stature,
And none dared cast an evil eye on him.
No one remained to stir up
Gossip, rumor, or strife.
Blue-gray like sharpened steel,
He grew keen and became lord of the nation.
He besieged and drove out
The hostile khagan, and became khan;
Whoever opposed him
Met his death there.
They properly placed the crown upon him,
And raised him onto the golden throne.
The two reins and single bridle
Were placed in Teñir’s hands,
Giving him rule over the khagan’s people.
At seven he was already full of ardor,
A giant among all the people of the earth.
Until he reached eight years,
He rode a stick and went on foot.
When Teñir reached nine,
He cast childhood away like a worn hide
And brought all Beijing beneath his command.
When he reached eleven,
His father Kite died.
When he reached twelve,
He buried his own father.
He made white deer serve like cattle,
And brought all Beijing beneath his command.
He had the tomb plated with yellow gold
And covered with cloth of gold;
He dug a resting place within the great mountain,
Excavating every feature in perfect measure,
A grave surpassing all others in the world.
He plated it with yellow gold,
Had the coiners praise their workmanship,
And the craftsmen fit everything together.
All around the great mountain
He enclosed it entirely with stone.
“So that no beast or living creature,
Not a single soul, may ever pass through;
And whoever ventures there unawares
May not remain alive,”
He set guards to watch it.
Surpassing all men in his deeds,
And following the Chinese rite
That beasts must not enter
And trample the place,
Lest they desecrate it,
Chyngteñir, whose hands knew
How to correct every flaw in the work,
Entrusted his father to warriors in jackets,
To pure men armored with stone,
To champions clad in mail,
And to many others,
Even to great tusked boars,
To guard his father.
“He truly is Teñir,” they said,
While old and young cried out in amazement.
Blessed by Kyzyr, he gained strength,
Seized the whole Chinese nation,
Drove them into a single hollow,
And packed them into a single pit.
When anyone died, he had the corpse
Cast into the fire and burned,
Enforcing his supreme decree.
Over the vast Chinese realm
And the many Kalmyk and Shibe peoples,
He became an absolute khan;
Whoever opposed him was slaughtered.
He was mounted upon the horse called Chyngteñir,
And Teñir remained to rule the nation.
Let us leave this tale here,
And from his forefather, Khan Tügöl,
Scion of an ancient land,
Let us begin the tidings from this side.
From the hero Semetey
Was born the hero Seytek.
He reached Talas safely,
Recovered the scattered herds,
Wrestled with his foes and took the khanate,
Then returned once more to Talas.
He became a man of weight,
A majestic khan,
Making the broad-backed Ala-Too
A settled and ordered homeland.
The ancestral realm left by his father
He tended wholly and made into a nation.
He turned every weakling into a man of substance,
And gave the homeless a homeland;
He made all his people skilled.
When weary, he had gazelles hunted,
And let the people live and play in ease.
While Seytek watched over them,
The people’s hearts were at peace,
And they became immensely wealthy.
He achieved all that he intended,
And filled every chest
With yellow gold and treasure.
They dressed in fox and sable,
And lived as though in the blessed Night of Power.
His people, countless in number, grew rich,
And the nation’s heart was at peace.
As they sat governing the people,
The leopards Seytek and Akjoltoy
Together served as ruling khans.
Such was the state of their people:
No outsider dared travel among them,
And none who attacked remained alive.
They stood like the barrier of Mount Kap,
Lions guarding their nation;
Thus did those noble men live.
Then, when the people began moving uphill,
At the season when horses’ coats turn dark,
When the grass had reached full growth,
The people headed for the summer pastures
And settled on the lower slopes;
The nation spread out and made camp.
The noble lady Bermet,
The renowned wife of Seytek,
Craved tiger meat in her pregnancy.
Her craving drove her to agitation,
For a wondrous child was within her,
And she could scarcely bear its force.
Learning of this, Akjoltoy
Struck down a bear far away.
For six days and then seven,
He was gone upon the hunt.
Yearning as he ranged the wilds,
He tirelessly rode for many days.
The khan’s courage waned as he searched the land,
Stirring turmoil in many places.
No tiger crossed his path,
And the quarry he sought could not be found.
Bewildered, he continued hunting,
Riding his horse until its flanks grew lean,
And roaming lands six fathoms wide.
He saw cliffs beyond the reach of sight,
And mountains like blue crags,
Driving argali and chasing wild asses;
Though he ranged far, he found nothing,
And Akjoltoy was sorely troubled.
Because of what had happened,
For the sake of unfortunate Bermet,
For the sake of that renowned lady,
He grieved at failing to find his quarry.
Wearied from his wandering,
Toward a jagged mountain spur,
To a pine-covered rocky headland
Whose mystery the mind could not fathom,
He turned his mount Kulunsur,
And Joltoy rode onward.
Over Kara-Kyya and Kapka-Tash,
The sun now set in darkness.
Sight faded and night fell,
As he crossed the black ridge.
There Joltoy stopped to camp.
From beneath him he took Kulunsur,
Removed the saddle and left him bare-backed,
Hobbled him securely,
Then sank into a giant’s sleep.
Using saddle and saddlecloth as a pillow,
He prayed to the Creator.
His snoring split the rocks,
The hero’s breath seemed to crack his head;
He slept in stillness, set like curds,
And plunged into resounding sleep.
When he woke with a start,
And turned onto his right side,
A striped tiger with a ringed tail
Was measuring Joltoy with its gaze,
Ready at that moment to strike.
The swift Kulunsur was urinating blood,
And from terror of the tiger
Had fallen senseless.
Behind that tiger,
A black dragon with a tiger’s head
Had drawn close beside it.
“It will tear me apart in an instant;
The man it seizes
Will be ground to dust.
My wandering here was in vain;
Will this life, a guest of seven days,
Now perish for nothing?”
His face turned yellow as straw,
And Akjoltoy, the equal of a countless army,
Stood there dumbfounded.
“What will become of my fate?
The creature behind me bears a mark
And may sting me and suck out my life.
If I do not take heed, I will die;
If it comes against me, a life will end.”
